clinicalPearls: Andersen disease (GSD IV) is an autosomal recessive deficiency of glycogen branching enzyme (GBE1), leading to accumulation of abnormal, poorly branched amylopectin-like glycogen (polyglucosan)

The classic hepatic form presents in infancy with failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly, and progressive liver cirrhosis with portal hypertension, often fatal in early childhood without transplantation
Unlike most hepatic glycogenoses, hypoglycaemia is not the dominant feature; progressive liver failure is
There is a wide phenotypic spectrum, including a severe neuromuscular perinatal or congenital form with hypotonia, contractures, and cardiomyopathy
An adult-onset variant, adult polyglucosan body disease, causes progressive neurogenic bladder, spasticity, peripheral neuropathy, and cognitive change
Diagnosis relies on demonstrating deficient branching enzyme activity and characteristic PAS-positive, partially diastase-resistant polyglucosan inclusions, confirmed by GBE1 genetics
Liver transplantation can be life-saving in the progressive hepatic form
reference.pathophysiology: Glycogen branching enzyme introduces the alpha-1,6 branch points that give glycogen its soluble, highly branched structure. In GSD IV, deficient GBE1 activity results in synthesis of an abnormal glycogen with few branch points, resembling amylopectin (polyglucosan). This insoluble material precipitates within cells and provokes tissue injury. In the liver it drives inflammation, fibrosis, and cirrhosis; in heart and skeletal muscle it produces cardiomyopathy and myopathy; and in the nervous system polyglucosan bodies accumulate in neurones and axons, underlying the neuromuscular and adult-onset neurological phenotypes.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of infantile cirrhosis and hepatosplenomegaly (e.g. neonatal haemochromatosis, tyrosinaemia, biliary atresia)
Congenital muscular dystrophies and congenital myopathies in the neuromuscular form
Lafora disease and other polyglucosan-related disorders
Adult-onset motor neurone disease or multiple sclerosis mimicking adult polyglucosan body disease
additionalInvestigations: Glycogen branching enzyme activity assay in leucocytes, fibroblasts, or liver
Liver biopsy showing PAS-positive, partially diastase-resistant polyglucosan inclusions and fibrosis/cirrhosis
Echocardiography and creatine kinase where cardiac or muscle involvement is suspected
MRI, nerve conduction studies, and urodynamics in suspected adult polyglucosan body disease
redFlags: Progressive hepatic decompensation with ascites, coagulopathy, or variceal bleeding
Failure to thrive with worsening hepatosplenomegaly in infancy
Cardiac failure or arrhythmia from cardiomyopathy
Severe neonatal hypotonia with contractures indicating the perinatal neuromuscular form
reference.prognosis: The classic progressive hepatic form is often fatal in early childhood without liver transplantation, whereas non-progressive hepatic and adult-onset forms have more variable, sometimes prolonged courses; the perinatal neuromuscular form carries a poor prognosis.
pitfalls: Expecting prominent hypoglycaemia and missing GSD IV, in which liver failure rather than hypoglycaemia dominates
Attributing infantile cirrhosis to more common hepatic causes without considering a glycogenosis
Not recognising adult polyglucosan body disease as part of the GBE1 spectrum
Confusing polyglucosan inclusions with other storage material without enzyme and genetic confirmation
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
